Binary search repeatedly halves a sorted range using lo/hi/mid; O(log n); requires sorted input
Worked trace of linear search and of binary search on a small array, verified in Bash

Best/worst/average case distinction for each search

claims.claim: Linear (sequential) search finds a target by checking elements one at a time until it is found or the collection ends.
Linear search runs in O(n) time; on average it examines about half the elements when the target is present.
Binary search searches a SORTED array by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half, comparing the target to the middle element and discarding the half that cannot contain it.
Binary search runs in O(log n) time.
Binary search requires the input to be sorted; correctness depends on that precondition, which is why library bisection tools document that the list must already be in sorted order.
A search is an application of an algorithm: a well-defined computational procedure that takes input and produces output.

For the sorted array [1,3,5,7,9,11], binary search for 7 first compares against the middle element 5 (index 2), then 9 (index 4), then 7 (index 3), finding index 3 in three comparisons; linear search for 9 in the same array takes five comparisons.
On a sorted array of 1,000,000 elements, worst-case linear search needs about 1,000,000 comparisons while binary search needs about 20 (floor(log2 n)+1).

conflictingEvidence.issue: NIST DADS writes binary search run time as 'O(ln n)'.
positions: NIST DADS: 'Run time is O(ln n).'
Standard CS convention and OpenStax: O(log n).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: In Big-O, the logarithm base is a constant factor, so O(ln n), O(log2 n), and O(log n) denote the same class. The lesson uses the conventional O(log n) and notes the base is immaterial under Big-O.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic boilerplate ('Searching is a foundational concept...', 'a label on a toolbox drawer') with no algorithmic content, no distinction between linear and binary search, and no complexity claims. None of it was usable as evidence.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate with the actual linear-vs-binary distinction, the sorted-input precondition, verified traces, and correct complexities (O(n) and O(log n)).
Added the sorting prerequisite handoff and a one-line hash-lookup contrast.
rightsIssues: NIST DADS and Python documentation are authoritative; facts synthesized and prose written originally. No source wording reproduced beyond short definitional phrases used for verification, not copied into the lesson.
